target.title: Customer onboarding drop-off
target.frame: A business scheduling product has many new accounts but fewer first published schedules than expected. Interviews from eight customers mention confusing setup, missing team information and postponement until the next roster cycle. Event logs record account creation, invitations, draft saves and publication, but do not capture offline preparation. The product team has one small release slot this month and needs a plan for deciding what to change and how to learn whether it helps.

instrument.state: A sample contains multiple components whose interactions with two phases differ enough that those components need not move together.
instrument.operation: Carry the sample through a system containing a moving phase and a stationary phase so that components repeatedly partition between them.
instrument.signal: Components migrate at different rates and emerge at different positions or times, producing separated bands or detector peaks.
instrument.inference: The separation pattern supports the presence of distinguishable components with different partition behavior and permits their relative retention to be characterized.
instrument.limit: Components with similar partition behavior may co-elute, operating conditions can shift retention, detector response may be nonspecific, and retention behavior alone generally does not establish chemical identity without appropriate standards or orthogonal evidence.

mapping.state: Act on a prospective cohort of newly created accounts, treating onboarding trajectories as a mixture of potentially distinguishable behaviors. Confusing setup, missing team information and waiting for a roster cycle are hypotheses suggested by eight interviews, not established segments or prevalence estimates. Assume accounts may repeatedly alternate between active product work and preparation or waiting; test that assumption rather than assigning each account a fixed cause.
mapping.operation: Use the same onboarding pathway and observation conditions across the initial cohort. Define the moving-phase counterpart as active work through invitations, draft saves and publication; define the stationary-phase counterpart as relatively persistent setup requirements and readiness constraints that can retain accounts before further progress. At successive milestones and a consistently timed inactivity follow-up, combine existing events with brief questions about the next required action, information availability, offline preparation and intended roster date. Record repeated progress–waiting–return transitions, allowing multiple or unknown reasons. Follow accounts through their stated next roster opportunity plus a predeclared grace period; use a fixed maximum follow-up for unknown dates and mark unfinished trajectories as censored. Before reviewing results, set minimum evidence and practically worthwhile improvement thresholds. Use the single small release slot for the smallest change addressing a recurrent, independently corroborated, product-addressable retention point: clearer instructions for verified comprehension problems, information collection support for verified preparation problems, or a timed return aid for verified postponement. If evidence does not distinguish an actionable constraint, use the slot for missing measurement instead. Where feasible, randomly assign eligible accounts to the selected change or the existing experience, keeping measurement identical. Stop recruitment and analysis at predeclared sample and follow-up limits; stop exposure early only under predefined harm criteria.
mapping.signal: Look for separated concentrations of trajectories in milestone position, time spent waiting, number of returns to active work and time to first publication. For example, renewed progress after obtaining team information or publication near a previously stated roster date would be candidate signals, not assumed observations. Report accounts with no return and incomplete follow-up alongside published accounts. In the release comparison, observe first-publication rates within a common window, time to publication, retention at the targeted checkpoint and predefined guardrails such as publication errors.
mapping.inference: Reproducible differences under common conditions would support distinguishable onboarding behaviors and characterize their relative retention at requirements or readiness constraints. Agreement between event patterns and contemporaneous preparation reports would strengthen a proposed mechanism. A sufficiently precise randomized improvement in first publication would support a causal effect of the tested change for the studied accounts and window; reduced delay at the targeted checkpoint would additionally support, but not establish, the proposed mechanism. Roll out only if the predeclared benefit and guardrail criteria are met. Otherwise retain the existing experience and use the uncertainty or conflicting evidence to specify the next targeted observation or test.
mapping.limit: Different causes can produce the same inactivity or publication timing, analogous to co-elution; one account can also experience several causes. Milestone events are nonspecific detectors, and absent events cannot distinguish abandonment from offline preparation. Added questions may change behavior, and self-reports may be incomplete. Roster timing, team size, acquisition mix and changes in onboarding conditions can shift apparent retention, so record these conditions and compare like observation windows. Behavioral retention alone does not identify a cause: seek corroboration through preparation reports, task observation or a controlled intervention. A small sample, sparse publications or censored accounts may leave effects unresolved; failure to meet the evidence threshold is not proof of no benefit. Without randomization, describe release differences as associations subject to confounding.
